meta.description: Year-wise sustainability activities mapped to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Edit this file to add, remove, or update activities. Each activity renders automatically on the website.

activities.title: Our Little Garden
activities.outcome: Children plant and care for a classroom herb garden, learning that living things need care and that we share our world with plants and minibeasts.

outcomes: I can name some things that plants need to grow.
I can help to look after a living plant.
I can say why plants and minibeasts are important to us.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 15, Life on Land, is about looking after the plants, animals and soil that we all share. Plants need sunlight, water and air to grow. When we care for plants, we also help tiny creatures like worms and bees.
lesson.handsOn: Children plant a herb seed or seedling in a small pot, water it and place it on a sunny windowsill. Each child draws a label for their plant and checks it every day, watering when the soil feels dry. Together the class keeps a simple picture diary of how the plant changes.
questions: What does your plant need every day to stay alive?
How can you tell if your plant is thirsty?
What might happen if we forgot to look after it?
Which minibeasts might like to live near our plants?
How does it feel to take care of a living thing?

activities.title: Every Drop Counts
activities.outcome: Pupils explore where water comes from and practise simple ways to save it, such as turning off the tap while brushing teeth.

outcomes: I can say where the clean water in our taps comes from.
I can name ways to use less water.
I can remember to turn off the tap so water is not wasted.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 6 is about clean water for everyone. Water travels to our taps through big pipes, and it is very precious. Some people in the world do not have clean water near their home, so we should try hard not to waste it.
lesson.handsOn: Using two bowls, children see how much water is wasted when a tap runs while brushing teeth, compared with turning it off. They practise the 'tap off' routine and design a small reminder sign to place near the class sink or their bathroom at home.
questions: Where does the water in our taps come from?
How did we waste water in our experiment?
What is one way you can save water at home?
Why is clean water so important for people?
Who could you teach to save water too?

activities.title: Sorting Superheroes
activities.outcome: Children learn to sort classroom waste into recycling streams and understand why keeping our school tidy helps our community.

outcomes: I can sort waste into the correct bin.
I can explain what recycling means.
I can say why a tidy school is better for everyone.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 11 is about making our towns and schools clean, safe and pleasant places to be. Recycling means turning old things like paper and plastic into new things instead of throwing them away. Sorting our rubbish carefully helps keep our community healthy.
lesson.handsOn: The class becomes 'Sorting Superheroes', using a set of clean, safe items to practise placing each one into the right recycling stream: paper, plastic and general waste. Teams race to sort correctly, then design a colourful bin label for the classroom.
questions: What does the word recycling mean?
Why do we put paper and plastic in different bins?
What could an old plastic bottle become next?
What might happen if everyone dropped their litter?
How can you be a Sorting Superhero at home?

activities.title: Save Our Seas
activities.outcome: Pupils discover how litter reaches the ocean and design posters encouraging their families to reduce single-use plastic.

outcomes: I can name some animals that live in the sea.
I can explain how litter can reach the ocean.
I can suggest one way to use less plastic.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 14, Life Below Water, is about protecting oceans and the creatures in them. Litter dropped on land can be blown or washed into rivers and out to sea, where it can harm animals like turtles and fish. Using less plastic helps keep the sea clean.
lesson.handsOn: Children watch a simple demonstration of 'litter' (paper pieces) travelling along a painted river into a bowl 'sea'. They then design a poster asking their families to swap one single-use plastic item, such as using a refillable bottle.
questions: Which sea animals can you name?
How might a plastic bag end up in the ocean?
Why is litter dangerous for sea creatures?
What plastic thing could your family stop using?
How could your poster help save the seas?

activities.title: From Seed to Snack
activities.outcome: Pupils grow vegetables in the school garden and track their growth, connecting healthy eating with where food comes from.

outcomes: I can explain what a plant needs to grow food.
I can describe where some of my food comes from.
I can help to grow and care for a food plant.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 2, Zero Hunger, is about making sure everyone has enough healthy food. Much of our food starts as a seed that grows with soil, water and sunlight. Understanding how food grows helps us to value it and waste less.
lesson.handsOn: Pupils plant fast-growing vegetables such as cress or beans and set up a growth chart, measuring and recording changes each week. They compare plants given different amounts of light or water to see what helps food grow best.
questions: What does a seed need to become a plant we can eat?
Where does the food on your plate really begin?
Why might some plants grow better than others?
How does growing food help to stop hunger?
What could we do with food we do not eat, instead of binning it?

activities.title: Waste Warriors
activities.outcome: Children audit the waste their class produces in a week and set a simple, measurable target to reduce it.

outcomes: I can measure how much waste my class makes.
I can suggest ways to make less waste.
I can set a simple goal to reduce waste.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 12 is about using things carefully so we do not waste them. Everything we throw away has to go somewhere, and making less waste protects the planet. Small changes, like reusing paper, add up to a big difference.
lesson.handsOn: Over one day, pupils collect and weigh (or count) the waste their class produces, sorting it into types. They discuss which items could be reduced, reused or recycled, then agree on one measurable class target for the following week.
questions: Which type of waste did our class make the most of?
Which items could we have reused instead?
Why does waste have to 'go somewhere'?
What target could help us to waste less next week?
How will we know if our plan has worked?

activities.title: Sunshine to Power
activities.outcome: Pupils build and test a simple solar-powered model, exploring how clean energy works and why it matters for the planet.

outcomes: I can explain what renewable energy means.
I can describe how solar power works in simple terms.
I can build and test a simple solar-powered model.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 7 is about clean energy that everyone can use. Renewable energy, like power from the sun, does not run out and does not pollute the air. Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity that we can use.
lesson.handsOn: Using a small solar panel and motor (or a solar toy kit), pupils build a simple model and test it in bright light and in shade. They record how the model behaves in different conditions and explain why sunshine matters for solar power.
questions: What does 'renewable' mean?
How does a solar panel make electricity?
Why did your model work better in bright light?
What could we power with the sun at school?
Why is clean energy better for the air we breathe?

activities.title: Weather Watchers
activities.outcome: Children record daily weather and discuss how the climate is changing, then agree on one class action to reduce their carbon footprint.

outcomes: I can record the weather accurately.
I can explain what climate change means in simple terms.
I can suggest an action to reduce our carbon footprint.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 13, Climate Action, is about protecting our planet from harmful changes to the climate. Burning fuels like petrol releases gases that warm the Earth, which can change our weather. The things we do every day, called our carbon footprint, can add to this or reduce it.
lesson.handsOn: Pupils record daily weather for a week using symbols and simple measurements, then discuss how weather and climate are different. As a class they choose one 'climate action', such as walking to school or switching off lights, and plan how to track it.
questions: What is the difference between weather and climate?
How can the things we do change the climate?
What is a carbon footprint?
Which class action could make the biggest difference?
How could we encourage others to join in?

activities.title: Clean Water Engineers
activities.outcome: Using a design-thinking process, pupils build and refine water-filtration devices, learning through iteration why access to clean water is a global challenge.

outcomes: I can explain why clean water is a global challenge.
I can design and build a simple water filter.
I can improve my design by testing and iterating.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 6 is about clean water and sanitation for all. Millions of people collect water that is not safe to drink. Engineers design filters that remove dirt and make water cleaner, and good design usually takes several attempts to get right.
lesson.handsOn: Working through a design-thinking process, pupils build a filter from materials such as sand, gravel, cotton wool and a plastic bottle to clean muddy water. They test how clear the water becomes, then redesign and retest to improve their result.
questions: Why is access to clean water not equal around the world?
How does each layer in your filter help?
What did you change after your first test, and why?
Could your filter make water safe to drink? How do you know?
How does thinking like an engineer help us solve real problems?

activities.title: Well-being Champions
activities.outcome: Pupils design a whole-class well-being routine and reflect on how physical activity and rest support healthy learning.

outcomes: I can explain what well-being means.
I can describe habits that support good health.
I can design a routine that helps our class feel well.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 3, Good Health and Well-being, is about helping everyone to live healthy lives. Well-being includes our bodies and our minds: sleep, movement, healthy food and time to relax all matter. Good habits help us to learn and to feel our best.
lesson.handsOn: Pupils explore how short bursts of movement and calm breathing affect how they feel, taking simple before-and-after measurements such as pulse or mood. They then design a daily class well-being routine and trial it for a week.
questions: What does well-being mean to you?
How did movement or calm breathing change how you felt?
Why does rest matter as much as exercise?
Which habit would help our class the most?
How could we keep our routine going every day?

activities.title: Upcycle Innovators
activities.outcome: Pupils redesign a discarded object into something useful, presenting their prototype and explaining the responsible-consumption thinking behind it.

outcomes: I can explain the difference between recycling and upcycling.
I can redesign a used object into something useful.
I can justify my design choices.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 12 is about responsible consumption: making and using things thoughtfully. Upcycling means giving a used item a new and better purpose instead of throwing it away. This saves resources and reduces waste.
lesson.handsOn: Pupils choose a clean, discarded object and use a design-thinking approach to redesign it into something useful, sketching ideas before building a prototype. They present their creation and explain the thinking behind each choice.
questions: How is upcycling different from recycling?
Why did you choose this object to transform?
What problem does your new design solve?
What would you improve if you made it again?
How could upcycling change the way we shop and throw things away?

activities.title: Reading Buddies
activities.outcome: Year 6 pupils lead reading sessions with younger children, exploring how quality education is something we can help share.

outcomes: I can explain why quality education matters for everyone.
I can support a younger child's reading.
I can reflect on what makes a good learning experience.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 4, Quality Education, is about making sure everyone can learn. Not every child in the world has access to good schooling. Sharing our skills, such as helping others to read, is one way we can support this goal in our own community.
lesson.handsOn: Year 6 pupils prepare and lead short reading sessions with younger children, choosing a book, asking questions and giving encouragement. Afterwards they reflect on what helped their buddy to enjoy reading and learn.
questions: Why is being able to read so important?
What did you do to help your buddy feel confident?
What makes a learning experience enjoyable?
How does teaching someone help you to learn too?
How could we widen access to reading across our school?

activities.title: Designing a Greener School
activities.outcome: Students use design thinking to map problems in their school environment and pitch a realistic sustainability improvement to staff.

outcomes: I can identify sustainability problems in my school environment.
I can apply a design-thinking process to propose a solution.
I can pitch my idea persuasively.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 11, Sustainable Cities and Communities, is about making the places we live and learn more sustainable. Schools use energy, water and materials, and small changes to buildings and habits can reduce their impact. Design thinking helps us move from a real problem to a workable solution.
lesson.handsOn: Students audit an area of the school, mapping sustainability problems such as wasted energy or litter. Using the design-thinking cycle, they generate ideas, sketch a solution and prepare a short, evidence-based pitch to staff.
questions: Which sustainability problem in our school matters most, and why?
Who is affected by this problem?
How does your solution address the root cause rather than the symptom?
What might make your idea difficult to put in place?
How would you measure whether your solution had worked?

activities.title: Biodiversity Survey
activities.outcome: Students survey plant and insect life on the school grounds, collecting simple data to argue for a wildlife-friendly area.

outcomes: I can explain what biodiversity means.
I can collect data through a fair survey.
I can use evidence to make a recommendation.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 15, Life on Land, includes protecting the variety of living things, known as biodiversity. A healthy environment has many different plants and animals living together. Surveying local wildlife helps us to understand and protect it.
lesson.handsOn: Students carry out a structured survey of plant and insect life in an area of the school grounds, using quadrats or timed counts to gather fair data. They present their findings and recommend a change to make the area more wildlife-friendly.
questions: What does biodiversity tell us about an environment's health?
How did you make sure your survey was fair?
What patterns did your data reveal?
What could reduce biodiversity in our area?
How would your recommendation help wildlife?

activities.title: The True Cost of Fast Fashion
activities.outcome: Students investigate the lifecycle of a garment and create a campaign encouraging more responsible consumption choices.

outcomes: I can describe the lifecycle of a garment.
I can evaluate the impact of fast fashion.
I can create a campaign for more responsible choices.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 12 is about responsible consumption and production. 'Fast fashion' means cheap clothes made quickly, often using large amounts of water and energy and creating waste. Understanding a garment's journey, from raw material to landfill, helps us to make better choices.
lesson.handsOn: Students trace the lifecycle of a typical garment, researching its environmental and human costs at each stage. They then design a short awareness campaign, such as a poster or social-post mock-up, encouraging more responsible fashion choices.
questions: What are the hidden costs behind a cheap T-shirt?
Which stage of a garment's life has the greatest impact?
Why do people keep buying fast fashion despite the costs?
What realistic changes could consumers make?
How could your campaign change someone's behaviour?

activities.title: Microplastics Investigation
activities.outcome: Students run a practical enquiry into microplastics and communicate their findings to raise awareness about ocean health.

outcomes: I can explain what microplastics are.
I can plan and carry out a fair investigation.
I can communicate scientific findings clearly.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 14, Life Below Water, includes reducing pollution such as microplastics: tiny plastic pieces that end up in oceans and food chains. They come from larger plastics breaking down and from products we use. Scientists investigate where they are found and how to reduce them.
lesson.handsOn: Students plan and run a practical enquiry, for example examining samples or testing how everyday products shed microplastics, controlling variables to keep it fair. They record results and present their findings with a clear conclusion.
questions: Where do microplastics come from?
How did you keep your investigation fair?
What do your results suggest about the scale of the problem?
Why are microplastics difficult to remove from the ocean?
What actions could reduce microplastic pollution?

activities.title: Our Carbon Footprint in Data
activities.outcome: Students collect and analyse data on their own carbon footprint, using data-driven decision-making to propose changes at home and school.

outcomes: I can define a carbon footprint.
I can collect and analyse data about my own impact.
I can use data to justify recommendations.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 13, Climate Action, calls for urgent action to combat climate change. A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases produced by our choices, such as travel, food and energy use. Analysing data helps us to target the changes that matter most.
lesson.handsOn: Students gather data on aspects of their own carbon footprint using a simple calculator or survey, then analyse it to find the biggest contributors. They use data-driven reasoning to propose realistic changes at home and school and predict the impact.
questions: What choices contribute most to a carbon footprint?
What does your data reveal that surprised you?
How reliable is the data you collected, and why?
Which change would give the greatest reduction for the least effort?
How could data persuade others to act?

activities.title: Innovation for Good
activities.outcome: Working in teams, students prototype a technology-based solution to a local sustainability challenge and evaluate its impact.

outcomes: I can explain how innovation can support sustainability.
I can prototype a solution to a local challenge.
I can evaluate my prototype against a need.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 9, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, is about building resilient systems and encouraging innovation. New technology can help to solve sustainability problems, from saving energy to reducing waste. Good innovation starts by understanding a real need.
lesson.handsOn: In teams, students identify a local sustainability challenge and prototype a technology-based solution, which might be physical, digital or a service. They test their prototype against the need and evaluate how well it performs.
questions: What real need does your innovation address?
Why is technology a good fit for this problem, or not?
What are the strengths and weaknesses of your prototype?
What unintended effects might your solution have?
How would you develop it further with more time or resources?

activities.title: Renewable Energy Engineering
activities.outcome: Students design, build and test small-scale renewable energy systems, evaluating efficiency and real-world viability.

outcomes: I can compare different renewable energy sources.
I can design, build and test a small-scale energy system.
I can evaluate efficiency and real-world viability.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 7 is about affordable and clean energy. Renewable sources such as solar, wind and hydro generate power without burning fossil fuels, though each has strengths and limitations. Engineers weigh efficiency, cost and practicality when designing energy systems.
lesson.handsOn: Students design and build a small-scale renewable energy system, such as a wind turbine or solar circuit, and measure its output under controlled conditions. They evaluate efficiency and discuss how viable their design would be at a larger scale.
questions: How do the main renewable sources compare on efficiency and cost?
What factors limited your system's output?
How did you measure efficiency, and how accurate was it?
What challenges arise when scaling a design up to a real setting?
Which renewable source best suits our region, and why?

activities.title: Mind Matters Campaign
activities.outcome: Students lead a peer mental-health awareness campaign, learning how well-being underpins a healthy school community.

outcomes: I can explain the link between well-being and a healthy community.
I can plan an evidence-informed awareness campaign.
I can evaluate the impact of my campaign.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 3, Good Health and Well-being, includes mental health. Looking after our minds is as important as our bodies, and open, informed conversations reduce stigma. Effective campaigns are based on evidence and reach their audience thoughtfully.
lesson.handsOn: Students research a well-being theme and plan a peer awareness campaign, deciding on message, audience and format. They deliver an element of it and gather simple feedback to evaluate its impact. Keep discussion general rather than personal, and signpost trusted sources of support.
questions: Why is mental well-being important for a whole community, not just individuals?
How can a campaign inform without causing harm or stigma?
Who is your audience, and how does that shape your message?
How will you know whether your campaign made a difference?
What responsibilities come with talking about well-being publicly?

activities.title: Sustainable Enterprise Challenge
activities.outcome: Students create a small enterprise built on sustainable principles, balancing profit with social and environmental responsibility.

outcomes: I can explain how enterprise can balance profit with responsibility.
I can develop a sustainable business idea.
I can justify decisions using the triple bottom line of people, planet and profit.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth, promotes fair, sustainable economic activity. A sustainable enterprise aims to make money while treating people fairly and protecting the environment, an idea often called the 'triple bottom line'. Trade-offs between these are common and must be managed.
lesson.handsOn: Students create a small enterprise concept built on sustainable principles, planning the product or service, its costs, and its social and environmental impact. They pitch it, justifying how it balances people, planet and profit.
questions: What does 'decent work' mean, and why does it matter?
Where does your enterprise face trade-offs between profit and responsibility?
How would you measure success beyond money?
Who benefits from your enterprise, and who might lose out?
Can a business be both profitable and genuinely sustainable? Defend your view.

activities.title: Climate Data Analysts
activities.outcome: Students interrogate real climate datasets and present evidence-based recommendations to the school leadership team.

outcomes: I can interpret real climate datasets.
I can identify trends and evaluate evidence.
I can present evidence-based recommendations.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 13, Climate Action, relies on evidence to guide decisions. Scientists gather large datasets on temperature, emissions and sea levels to identify trends. Interpreting data critically, including its limitations, is essential to making sound recommendations.
lesson.handsOn: Students interrogate a real climate dataset, using graphs and simple statistics to identify trends and anomalies. They evaluate the reliability of the data and prepare evidence-based recommendations to present to the school leadership team.
questions: What trends can you identify in the data, and how confident are you?
What are the limitations or biases in this dataset?
How do you distinguish correlation from causation here?
Which recommendation does the evidence most strongly support?
How should uncertainty be communicated to decision-makers?

activities.title: Smart, Sustainable Cities
activities.outcome: Students explore how AI and data can make cities more sustainable, producing a critical proposal that weighs benefits against ethical concerns.

outcomes: I can evaluate how data and AI can support sustainable cities.
I can weigh benefits against ethical concerns.
I can construct a reasoned proposal.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 11 is about sustainable cities and communities. Smart technologies and AI can reduce energy use, manage transport and cut waste, but they also raise concerns about privacy, equity and over-reliance on data. A strong proposal weighs both the opportunities and the risks.
lesson.handsOn: Students explore a real smart-city application and develop a critical proposal for using data or AI to make a city more sustainable. They must set out the benefits, the ethical risks and the safeguards, and defend their position.
questions: Which sustainability problems can smart technology realistically solve?
What ethical risks accompany data-driven cities?
Who might be excluded or disadvantaged, and how could that be addressed?
How should the balance between efficiency and privacy be struck?
Is more technology always the answer? Justify your view.

activities.title: Community Partnerships Project
activities.outcome: Students partner with a local organisation on a sustainability initiative, learning that lasting change relies on collaboration.

outcomes: I can explain why partnerships are essential to sustainable change.
I can plan and manage a collaborative project.
I can evaluate the impact of the partnership.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 17, Partnerships for the Goals, recognises that lasting change needs collaboration between people and organisations. Working with a partner brings new expertise, resources and reach. Successful partnerships depend on shared goals, communication and trust.
lesson.handsOn: Students partner with a local organisation on a genuine sustainability initiative, agreeing shared aims, roles and a timeline. They carry out the project and evaluate what the partnership achieved and what they learned.
questions: Why can partnerships achieve more than working alone?
What did each partner contribute that the other could not?
What tensions or challenges arose, and how did you manage them?
How do you measure the success of a partnership?
What makes a partnership sustainable beyond a single project?

activities.title: Peer Sustainability Mentors
activities.outcome: Students design and deliver sustainability lessons to younger year groups, developing leadership while spreading quality education.

outcomes: I can plan and deliver effective teaching on sustainability.
I can adapt content for a younger audience.
I can reflect critically on my leadership.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 4, Quality Education, includes lifelong learning and the sharing of knowledge. Teaching others deepens our own understanding and builds leadership. Effective teaching means adapting content, checking understanding and inspiring action.
lesson.handsOn: Students design and deliver a short sustainability lesson to a younger year group, planning clear outcomes, an activity and questions. Afterwards they gather feedback and critically reflect on their teaching and leadership.
questions: What makes teaching about sustainability effective for younger learners?
How did you adapt complex ideas without losing accuracy?
How did you check that your learners understood?
What did leading this teach you about your own understanding?
How could peer teaching create lasting change in a school?

activities.title: Youth Voice Forum
activities.outcome: Students research a sustainability policy issue and present a reasoned position at a student forum, practising evidence-based advocacy.

outcomes: I can research a sustainability policy issue rigorously.
I can construct a reasoned, evidence-based argument.
I can engage respectfully with opposing views.
lesson.knowledge: Goal 16, Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions, includes fair decision-making and the right to be heard. Sustainability often involves contested choices where evidence and values meet. Advocacy means arguing a case clearly while listening to and respecting other perspectives.
lesson.handsOn: Students research a sustainability policy issue, build an evidence-based position and present it at a student forum or debate. They must respond to questions and engage constructively with opposing arguments.
questions: What evidence most strongly supports your position?
How do values, as well as facts, shape this debate?
What is the strongest argument against your view, and how do you answer it?
Who holds power over this decision, and who is affected by it?
How can young people's voices genuinely influence policy?
